reference.source: ILAE classification and clinical guidance on the epilepsy syndromes
clinicalPearls: A common self-limited focal epilepsy of early childhood dominated by autonomic seizures, especially emesis.
Onset is typically 3 to 6 years; seizures are infrequent but often prolonged, amounting to autonomic status epilepticus.

A typical event comprises nausea, retching and vomiting with pallor, eye deviation and impaired responsiveness, frequently arising from sleep and sometimes progressing to a hemiconvulsion or generalised convulsion.
Additional autonomic features include pupillary changes, incontinence, hypersalivation and cyanosis.
Interictal EEG classically shows multifocal, shifting spikes, often occipital, but the distribution is variable and the EEG may be normal.
Neurological examination, development and neuroimaging are normal.
Because seizures are infrequent, long-term daily medication is often unnecessary and a rescue plan for prolonged seizures is central to management.
Prognosis is excellent, with spontaneous remission within a year or two of onset.
reference.pathophysiology: Panayiotopoulos syndrome is regarded as a benign, maturation-dependent focal epilepsy reflecting a diffuse, age-related cortical hyperexcitability with a predilection for autonomic networks. The prominent emetic and autonomic features are attributed to epileptic activation of central autonomic networks, particularly insular and anterior regions, while the shifting, often posterior EEG foci indicate widespread rather than fixed epileptogenicity that resolves with brain maturation.
additionalDifferentials: Encephalitis, considered during prolonged autonomic status
additionalInvestigations: MRI brain if features are atypical or the examination is abnormal
Blood glucose and basic metabolic screen during an acute event
ECG to exclude cardiac syncope or arrhythmia
Lumbar puncture if encephalitis is suspected during prolonged status
redFlags: Autonomic status epilepticus with a seizure lasting beyond thirty minutes
Focal neurological deficit or abnormal development
An atypical or fixed occipital lesion on imaging
Recurrent seizures deviating from the expected benign course
reference.prognosis: Excellent: the disorder is self-limited with remission usually within one to two years of onset and normal long-term cognitive and neurological outcome, although a minority later develop other seizure types.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing prolonged autonomic seizures as encephalitis, gastroenteritis or syncope.
Over-treating an essentially benign, infrequent-seizure condition with long-term medication.
Failing to provide a rescue plan for prolonged seizures.
Confusing it with late-onset (Gastaut) occipital epilepsy, which causes visual seizures and follows a different course.
references: ILAE position papers on classification of the epilepsies
Panayiotopoulos CP. A Clinical Guide to Epileptic Syndromes and their Treatment
management: Reassurance and education, since the syndrome is self-limited and many children do not require regular anti-seizure medication
Rescue benzodiazepine such as buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam for prolonged seizures or autonomic status epilepticus
Maintenance anti-seizure medication such as carbamazepine, levetiracetam or valproate only if seizures are frequent or distressing
First-aid guidance for parents on the recovery position and timing of seizures
Distinguish acute events from cardiac and metabolic causes and treat accordingly during episodes
Developmental and neurological follow-up with the expectation of remission within a couple of years
